First Steps

Python basics, part 1 of 6

Python First Steps

This page takes you from nothing to small working programs: running Python, printing, storing values in variables, working with numbers and making decisions with if. It is a Python 3 rewrite of the opening Pythofrank lessons from February 2017. The number and if-else examples are the original ones, updated from Python 2.7. The rest is written fresh.

Getting started

Group 1 of 4 · running Python and showing output

Before writing programs you need to know what Python is, how to start it and how to make it show something on the screen.

  • What Python is: the language and where it is used
  • Running Python: interactive mode and script files
  • Showing output with print: values, separators and f-strings
  • Comments: notes for the person reading the code

What Python is

Python is a general purpose programming language, first released by Guido van Rossum in 1991. Its code reads close to plain English, which makes it a common first language.

Python is interpreted: a program called the interpreter reads your code and runs it directly, so there is no separate compile step. It is also dynamically typed: you do not declare the type of a variable, Python works it out from the value.

Where it is usedExamples
Web back endsDjango, Flask, FastAPI
Data analysis and machine learningpandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch
Automation and scriptingrenaming files, calling APIs, scheduled jobs
Testing and toolingpytest, command line tools
Teachingschools, universities, coding interviews

Version: this site uses Python 3. Python 2, which the 2017 lessons were written for, reached its end of life in 2020 and should not be used for new code.

Running Python

First check that Python is installed. Open a terminal and ask for the version. On macOS and Linux the command is usually python3. On Windows it is often python or py.

If the command is not found, install Python from python.org and try again.

Interactive mode

Type python3 on its own to start interactive mode. The >>> prompt waits for one statement, runs it and shows the result straight away. It is the quickest way to try an idea.

A script file

For anything you want to keep, save the code in a file ending in .py and pass the file name to Python. The file is run from the first line to the last.

Difference: interactive mode shows the value of any expression you type. A script shows nothing unless you call print().

Showing output with print

print() writes values to the screen. Give it several values separated by commas and it puts one space between them and a new line at the end.

Concept: a string with f before the opening quote is an f-string. Python replaces each {...} inside it with the value of the expression. :.2f means two digits after the decimal point.

Comments

A comment is a note for people. Python ignores everything from # to the end of the line. Use comments to say why the code does something, not to repeat what it plainly does.

Building blocks

Group 2 of 4 · the rules every Python file follows

These chapters cover how values are named, how they come in from the keyboard and how Python expects code to be laid out.

  • Variables and names: giving a value a name
  • Input and type conversion: reading text and turning it into numbers
  • Indentation: spaces that are part of the syntax
  • Quotation: single, double and triple quotes
  • Statements and lines: long statements and short ones

Variables and names

A variable is a name that points to a value. It is created the moment you assign to it with =. There is nothing to declare first, and the same name can later point to a value of another type.

Naming rules

RuleFineNot allowed
Letters, digits and underscore onlyaccount_noaccount-no, account no
Cannot start with a digitaccount22account
Cannot be a keywordclass_nameclass, if, for, return
Upper and lower case differbalance and Balance are two separate names

Convention: write variable names in lower case with underscores between words (opening_balance), and values that never change in capitals (MIN_BALANCE = 1000). Choose names that say what the value means.

Input and type conversion

input() shows a prompt, waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, and returns what was typed. This block waits for the keyboard, so it is not run by the site's checker.

input() always returns a string, which is Python's type for text. To do arithmetic you must convert it. int(), float() and str() make a new value of that type.

Remember: a conversion that cannot work raises a ValueError. The try and except used here to catch it are explained in Python Errors and Files.

Indentation

Many languages mark a block of code with braces. Python uses indentation, the spaces at the start of a line. A line ending in a colon opens a block, and every line indented under it belongs to that block.

Wrong indentation is not a style problem, it is an error. Python refuses to start this file, which is why the block is not run here.

Convention: use 4 spaces for each level and never mix tabs with spaces. Most editors insert 4 spaces when you press Tab in a .py file.

Quotation

Text goes between quotes. Single and double quotes mean exactly the same thing, so pick the one that does not appear in your text. Three quotes in a row start a string that may run over several lines.

Concept: a triple quoted string keeps its line breaks. The same form, placed as the first statement of a function or file, is used as its documentation.

Statements and lines

Normally one line holds one statement. A statement that is too long can continue on the next line in two ways: inside any open bracket, or after a backslash at the very end of the line.

The opposite is also possible. A semicolon separates several statements on one line.

Advice: prefer brackets to the backslash, because a single space after a backslash breaks it. Keep one statement per line in real code. The semicolon form is shown so you can read it, not so you write it.

Numbers

Group 3 of 4 · number types and arithmetic

These chapters follow the 2017 Numbers lesson. The same values are used, with the results Python 3 gives.

  • Number types: int, float and complex
  • Arithmetic: the operators, including //, % and **
  • Floats and complex numbers: arithmetic that is not exact
  • Converting numbers: from one number type to another
  • The math module: square roots, rounding and constants

Number types

Python has three built-in number types. An int is a whole number. A float has a decimal point. A complex number has a real part and an imaginary part, written with j. type() tells you which one a value is.

Python 2: the old lesson also had a long type, written 256L. Python 3 has no long. Every whole number is an int of unlimited size, and 256L is a syntax error.

Arithmetic

The usual operators work as in school maths. Three need a closer look: // divides and rounds down to a whole number, % gives the remainder, and ** raises to a power.

Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction, and ** before all of them. Brackets change the order. An operator followed by = updates a variable in place.

Python 2: in the 2017 lesson 4 / 5 gave 0, because dividing two whole numbers threw the fraction away. In Python 3 / always gives a float. Use // when you want the whole number.

Floats and complex numbers

The same operators work on floats. A float is stored in binary with a fixed number of digits, so some decimal values cannot be held exactly and a tiny error can show up at the end.

Complex numbers support +, -, *, / and **.

Money: never compare floats with == after arithmetic, and do not keep money in a float. Store whole paise or cents in an int, or use Decimal from the decimal module. Python 2: the old lesson used % on complex numbers. Python 3 removed that and raises a TypeError.

Converting numbers

Calling a type like a function makes a new number of that type. int() cuts off the fraction. round() goes to the nearest value instead.

Surprise: round(4.5) is 4, not 5. Python rounds an exact half to the nearest even number, which keeps long sums from drifting upwards.

The math module

A module is a file of ready made code. import math loads the standard maths module, and its functions are then used as math.name. A few number functions are built in and need no import.

Decisions

Group 4 of 4 · running code only when a condition holds

A program becomes useful when it can choose what to do. These chapters follow the 2017 If else lesson and then add the pieces it left out.

  • if and else: one of two paths
  • elif: one of several paths
  • Comparison and logical operators: building conditions
  • Truthiness: values that count as true or false
  • The conditional expression: a choice on one line

if and else

if checks a condition. When it is true the indented block under it runs. When it is false the block under else runs instead. The else part is optional.

Careful: = stores a value, == compares two values. Writing if a = 10: is a syntax error.

elif

elif is short for "else if". Python checks the conditions from the top and runs the block of the first one that is true. The rest are skipped, even if they are true as well.

An if can sit inside another if. Each level is indented by 4 more spaces.

Order matters: put the most specific condition first. If amount > balance came after a wider check that is also true, it would never be reached.

Comparison and logical operators

A comparison gives True or False, the two values of the bool type. Logical operators join comparisons into larger conditions.

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
==equal to5 == 5.0True
!=not equal to5 != 3True
< >less than, greater than3 > 10False
<= >=less or equal, greater or equal5 <= 5True
andtrue when both sides are true5 > 3 and 5 > 9False
ortrue when at least one side is true5 > 3 or 5 > 9True
notturns true into false and backnot 5 > 3False
inis inside a collection or string"kesh" in "Rishikesh"True

and and or stop as soon as the answer is known. This is called short circuiting, and it lets the first check protect the second one.

Precedence: not is applied first, then and, then or. When a condition mixes them, add brackets so nobody has to remember that.

Truthiness

The condition after if does not have to be a comparison. Any value can be used, and Python treats it as true or false. Zero, empty collections, the empty string and None count as false. Everything else counts as true.

Concept: None is Python's value for "nothing here". Test for it with is None or is not None, not with ==.

The conditional expression

When an if and else only choose between two values, the choice fits on one line: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false.

Advice: use this form for a short choice between two values. If either side needs more than a simple expression, the normal if block is easier to read.
